--- title: "5. Long-run risks: the endowment" aliases: - /long-run-risks-model.html --- [Chapter 4](04-epstein-zin-preferences.qmd) built an investor whose marginal utility responds to news about future consumption. The preferences are worthless if there is no such news. If consumption growth is white noise, there is nothing persistent to learn about, and the Epstein-Zin kernel prices almost exactly like the power-utility kernel it replaced. The chapter supplies the other half, an endowment in which expected growth genuinely moves. The design comes from Bansal and Yaron (2004), and the idea fits in one sentence. Consumption growth carries a small, highly persistent component under transitory noise. The persistent component is tiny, a few tenths of a percent per month, and it is nearly invisible in any given year. A shock to it, however, is news about the next decade of consumption rather than about the current year. The investor of Chapter 4 prefers early resolution of uncertainty, so persistent news is the kind she fears. Claims whose cash flows are levered to it must pay a premium. The same four equations also carry the entire cross section. Growth, value, and market portfolios will differ in exactly one economically meaningful way, which is how strongly their dividends load on the persistent component. The loading, called cash-flow leverage, is the model's characteristic and serves the purpose the CAPM assigns to beta. It is a property of dividends, and it is measurable without ever touching a return. ## Four equations The endowment and the cash flows are (paper eq. 6): $$ \Delta c_{t+1} = \mu_c + x_t + \sigma_t\, \eta_{t+1} $$ {#eq-cons} $$ x_{t+1} = \rho\, x_t + \varphi_x\, \sigma_t\, \epsilon_{t+1} $$ {#eq-x} $$ \sigma_{t+1}^2 = \bar\sigma^2 (1-\nu) + \nu\, \sigma_t^2 + \sigma_w\, w_{t+1} $$ {#eq-vol} $$ \Delta d_{i,t+1} = \mu_i + \phi_i\, x_t + \varphi_{\sigma,i}\, \sigma_t\, u_{i,t+1} $$ {#eq-div} with all shocks standard normal. In words, line by line: - @eq-cons: the current month's consumption growth is a constant trend $\mu_c$, plus where expected growth currently stands ($x_t$), plus transitory noise. $x_t$ is the deviation of expected growth from its mean, and it is the time-varying counterpart of the constant $g$ a DCF plugs into its terminal value. - @eq-x: expected growth itself drifts slowly. The persistence $\rho$ is the model's most consequential parameter. The innovations are small ($\varphi_x$ scales them well below the transitory shock) but their effects last. - @eq-vol: the volatility of everything is itself a slow-moving state. Economic uncertainty rises and recedes with persistence $\nu$ around the mean level $\bar\sigma^2$. The second state variable will price a distinct risk, but $x_t$ does the work in the current chapter. - @eq-div: each claim $i$ pays dividends whose growth inherits expected consumption growth with **leverage** $\phi_i$, plus idiosyncratic noise scaled by $\varphi_{\sigma,i}$ (the residual $u_{i,t+1}$ correlates with the consumption shock $\eta_{t+1}$ at a rate $\alpha_i$). $\phi_i$ is the only parameter in the whole model that differs across claims in an economically central way. Table II sets $\phi = 2.6$ for growth, $6.2$ for value, and $2.8$ for the market. A value firm's cash flows are levered to long-run news more than twice as strongly as a growth firm's. Everything the rest of the course says about the value premium follows from the one contrast. ## How long a shock to expected growth lasts The persistence $\rho = 0.98$ is at a monthly frequency. Compute the half-life of a shock to expected growth: ::: {#bf4930d9 .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import numpy as np import lrrcs as lrr cons = lrr.get_table_ii_params().cons half_life = np.log(0.5) / np.log(cons.rho) print(f"rho = {cons.rho} (monthly) => " f"half-life of x_t = {half_life:.1f} months") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` rho = 0.98 (monthly) => half-life of x_t = 34.3 months ``` ::: ::: A piece of news about expected growth still has half its force three years later. The persistence is what separates @eq-x from noise. The innovation to $x_t$ is on the order of $\varphi_x \sigma \approx$ two hundredths of a percent per month, which is invisible next to the transitory shock, but it compounds over a decade of expected consumption. The investor of Chapter 4 prices news by its total future weight rather than by its size in the current month. ## The persistence in the data The i.i.d. benchmark is testable, because white-noise growth has zero autocorrelation. Annual U.S. consumption growth does not: ::: {#85e7b428 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} # Data bootstrap: use the repo's committed CSVs, or fetch them when this # notebook runs outside the repository. from pathlib import Path import urllib.request DATA = Path("../../data") if not DATA.exists(): DATA = Path("data") DATA.mkdir(exist_ok=True) base = ("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/tlorans/" "kiku-value-premium-replication/main/data/") for f in ("consumption_annual.csv",): if not (DATA / f).exists(): urllib.request.urlretrieve(base + f, DATA / f) ``` ::: ::: {#661f02b9 .cell execution_count=3} ``` {.python .cell-code} import pandas as pd dc = pd.read_csv(DATA / "consumption_annual.csv")["dc"] print(f"{len(dc)} years of annual consumption growth") print(f"first autocorrelation (AC1): {dc.autocorr(1):.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 74 years of annual consumption growth first autocorrelation (AC1): 0.41 ``` ::: ::: An AC1 of 0.41 in 74 years of data is a clear rejection of white noise. Growth in one year carries information about growth in the next. The AC1 does not by itself prove the two-component structure of @eq-cons and @eq-x. A persistent component of the calibrated size is hard to detect, and the difficulty is the standing objection to the whole approach, taken up in [Chapter 9](09-the-market-test.qmd). The AC1 is, however, one of the moments the calibration below is fit to, and the simulation at the end of the chapter reproduces it. ## The calibration in one table Every number below is read from `lrr.get_table_ii_params()` at run time, which is the same object every solver in the course consumes. Units are monthly. ::: {#28ed3201 .cell execution_count=4} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} import pandas as pd from great_tables import GT KIKU_GT = dict(table_background_color="transparent", table_font_size="0.92rem", heading_title_font_size="1.05rem", heading_subtitle_font_size="0.85rem", source_notes_font_size="0.8rem", column_labels_font_weight="bold", data_row_padding="4px") p = lrr.get_table_ii_params() prefs, c = p.prefs, p.cons calib_df = pd.DataFrame({ "block": ["Preferences (household)"] * 4 + ["Consumption process (endowment)"] * 6, "parameter": ["delta", "gamma", "psi", "theta", "mu", "rho", "phi_x", "sigma", "nu", "sigma_w"], "value": [f"{prefs.delta}", f"{prefs.gamma}", f"{prefs.psi}", f"{prefs.theta:.1f}", f"{c.mu}", f"{c.rho}", f"{c.phi_x}", f"{c.sigma}", f"{c.nu}", f"{c.sigma_w}"], "meaning": ["time preference", "risk aversion", "elasticity of intertemporal substitution", "derived, (1 - gamma) / (1 - 1/psi)", "mean monthly growth (about 1.8 %/yr)", "persistence of x_t (half-life about 3 yrs)", "sd of x_t shocks, relative to sigma", "mean monthly volatility (about 2.2 %/yr)", "persistence of volatility", "sd of volatility shocks"], }) ( GT(calib_df, rowname_col="parameter", groupname_col="block") .tab_header(title="Table II calibration, monthly units") .cols_label(value="value", meaning="meaning") .tab_source_note("Read from lrr.get_table_ii_params() at build time.") .tab_options(**KIKU_GT) ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=4} ```{=html}

``` ::: ::: Read the tables with the firewall in mind. The preference block and the consumption block are disciplined by aggregate moments only: the mean, volatility, and autocorrelation of consumption growth, and the risk-free rate. The cash-flow block is disciplined by dividends only. [Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd) estimates the leverages $\phi_i$ by regressing dividend growth on a moving average of consumption growth, with no returns anywhere in the procedure. Returns appear once, at the very end of the course, as the thing to be explained. ## What a path looks like Numbers on a page understate how well hidden $x_t$ is. Simulate forty years of the economy and plot monthly consumption growth against the expected-growth state underneath it: ::: {#283d4af1 .cell execution_count=6} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} from plotnine import (ggplot, aes, geom_line, geom_hline, labs, scale_color_manual, theme_minimal, theme, element_blank, element_line, element_text) sim = lrr.Dynamics(lrr.get_table_ii_params(), seed=3).simulate_cashflows(480) path_df = pd.DataFrame({ "years": np.arange(480) / 12, "realized": 100 * sim["dc"], "expected": 100 * (cons.mu + sim["x"]), }) plot = ( ggplot(path_df, aes("years")) + geom_line(aes(y="realized", color='"realized growth Δc"'), size=0.5) + geom_line(aes(y="expected", color='"expected growth μ + x"'), size=0.9) + geom_hline(yintercept=100 * cons.mu, color="#1b1714", linetype="dotted", size=0.4) + scale_color_manual(values={"realized growth Δc": "#b0aca6", "expected growth μ + x": "#7a1f1f"}) + labs(x="years", y="monthly growth (%)") + theme_minimal(base_size=11) + theme(figure_size=(6.5, 3.4), text=element_text(color="#2d2926"), panel_grid_minor=element_blank(), panel_grid_major=element_line(color="#e2d6c4", size=0.4), axis_line=element_line(color="#1b1714", size=0.5), legend_title=element_blank(), legend_position="top") ) plot.show() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display} ![Forty years of simulated monthly consumption growth (gray) and the expected-growth component μ_c + x_t underneath it (dark red). The persistent state is an order of magnitude smaller than the noise, yet it carries the priced risk.](05-long-run-risks_files/figure-html/cell-7-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: The gray series is what an econometrician observes, and the dark line is the state the investor is afraid of. Distinguishing the second inside the first from a few decades of data is genuinely hard, and the paper does not claim otherwise. The model claims that prices respond to the dark line, which is why valuations will turn out to be informative about $x_t$ in a way realized consumption is not. ## Simulation to annual data: a warning about aggregation One detail affects every comparison of the model's monthly output to annual data, and skipping it corrupts the comparison. The paper builds annual consumption the way NIPA builds it. First, sum twelve monthly levels to an annual level. Then take log growth of the annual sums. The level construction is not the same as summing twelve monthly log growth rates, and the difference is visible in exactly the moment the chapter uses: ::: {#00cb9b56 .cell execution_count=7} ``` {.python .cell-code code-fold="true"} dyn = lrr.Dynamics(lrr.get_table_ii_params(), seed=0) dc_m = dyn.simulate_cashflows(12 * 20000)["dc"] # NIPA convention: annual level = sum of 12 monthly levels, then log growth level = np.exp(np.cumsum(dc_m)) annual_level = level.reshape(-1, 12).sum(axis=1) g_levels = np.diff(np.log(annual_level)) # Naive alternative: sum the 12 monthly log growth rates g_logs = dc_m.reshape(-1, 12).sum(axis=1)[1:] def ac1(y): return np.corrcoef(y[:-1], y[1:])[0, 1] print(f"model annual consumption growth, 20,000 simulated years") print(f" AC1, aggregating levels (NIPA convention): {ac1(g_levels):.2f}") print(f" AC1, summing log growth rates: {ac1(g_logs):.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` model annual consumption growth, 20,000 simulated years AC1, aggregating levels (NIPA convention): 0.43 AC1, summing log growth rates: 0.20 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.callout-warning title="Time-aggregate levels, not log growth"} The same simulated economy prints an annual AC1 of 0.43 when monthly levels are summed within the year, and only 0.20 when monthly log growth rates are summed. The 0.43 matches the model AC1 in the paper's Table III and sits next to the 0.41 measured in the data above. Summing levels within the year overlaps adjacent years' information and adds persistence that the log-growth aggregation throws away. A simulation that sums log growth will understate the paper's annual autocorrelation every time. It is the single most common way to fail to reproduce Table III. ::: ## Takeaways - The endowment is four equations: persistent expected growth $x_t$ inside consumption growth, slowly moving uncertainty $\sigma_t^2$, and dividends levered to $x_t$ claim by claim. - $x_t$ is small but long lasting. With $\rho = 0.98$ monthly, a shock keeps half its force after 34 months, and long-run news is what the Chapter 4 investor prices. - The data reject white-noise consumption growth. Annual AC1 is 0.41 in 74 years, and the calibrated model reproduces it (0.43) under the correct level aggregation. - The cross section enters through one parameter, the cash-flow leverage $\phi_i$ (growth 2.6, market 2.8, value 6.2). It is a property of dividends, estimated in [Chapter 8](08-calibrating-cash-flows.qmd) without returns. ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Recall"} Answer from memory before opening. 1. Name the four equations of the endowment in words. 2. How long does a shock to expected growth keep half its force at $\rho = 0.98$ monthly? 3. Across the three claims, exactly one parameter differs in an economically central way. Which, and what does it measure? **Answers.** 1. Consumption growth carries a persistent expected-growth component plus noise; expected growth drifts with persistence $\rho$; volatility itself moves slowly; and each claim's dividend growth loads on the persistent component with leverage $\phi_i$. 2. About 34 months, three years. 3. The cash-flow leverage $\phi_i$: how strongly the claim's dividend growth moves with the persistent component of consumption (2.6 growth, 2.8 market, 6.2 value). ::: ## Exercises 1. Recompute the half-life of $x_t$ for $\rho = 0.95$ and $\rho = 0.90$. Then look ahead to the elasticity $A_1 = (\phi - 1/\psi)/(1 - \kappa_1 \rho)$ of [Chapter 6](06-log-linear-solution.qmd) and say, before computing anything, which claim's valuation loses more when persistence falls. 2. Rerun the aggregation cell with `phi_x = 0` (rebuild the parameters with `lrr.ConsumptionParams(phi_x=0.0)` inside a `ModelParams`). With no persistent component at all, what AC1 does each aggregation convention print, and what does the gap between them tell you about the level convention on its own? 3. Simulate two economies with `lrr.Dynamics(..., seed=7)`, identical except $\rho = 0.98$ versus $\rho = 0.90$, and plot $\mu_c + x_t$ for both. How does the figure change, and at which frequency would you now look for the state in the data? ::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Check your answer"} ::: {#6c3beded .cell execution_count=8} g_lvl[1:])[0,1]:.2f}") print(f"AC1, log convention: {np.corrcoef(g_log[:-1], g_log[1:])[0,1]:.2f}") ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` rho = 0.95: half-life = 13.5 months rho = 0.9: text=element_text(color="#2d2926"), panel_grid_minor=element_blank(), panel_grid_major=element_line(color="#e2d6c4", size=0.4), axis_line=element_line(color="#1b1714", size=0.5), Lower persistence turns the slow swings into quick fades.](05-long-run-risks_files/figure-html/cell-10-output-1.svg){} ::: ::: The half-life falls from 34 months to about 14 at rho = 0.95 and about 7 at rho = 0.90, and the claim that loses most is value, whose phi puts the most of its valuation on the persistent state. With phi_x = 0 the log convention prints a near-zero AC1 but the level convention still prints 0.24, so the overlap in the level construction adds persistence on its own. Reaching the 0.43 the paper reports needs the persistent component on top of the convention. The figure shows the state decaying quickly at rho = 0.90, so you would look for it in shorter moving averages. ::: ::: {.firewall} **Where each number comes from.** The half-life, the calibration tables, the simulated figure, and both AC1 prints come from `lrr.get_table_ii_params()` and `lrr.Dynamics(...).simulate_cashflows` in the cells above. The data AC1 of 0.41 is computed from `data/consumption_annual.csv`.
